title: Experiences of oldest-old caregivers whose partner is approaching end-of-life: a mixed-method systematic review and narrative synthesis
author: Tessa Morgan

steps_raw.instruction: Experiences of older caregivers whose partner is approaching end of life: a mixed-method systematic review and narrative synthesis
Population or Perspective: Carers or caregivers or spouses or supporters over 75, of a spouse who has an advanced and life-limiting condition.

Spousal caregivers were partners (whether married or not) who were “in a close supportive role who share in the illness experience of the patient and who undertake vital care work and emotion management” (NICE, 2004).

“End-of-life” refers to the chronologically indefinite part of life when patients and their caregivers are encountering the implications such as symptoms and practical support needs of an advanced chronic or progressive life-limiting illness (Gaertner et al. 2017, Lorenz et al., 2005).
Studies focusing on dementia were only included if they reported on moderate to severe stages of the illness.

Interventional studies were not included as we were interested in the experiences of very old spousal caregivers in their naturally occurring setting rather than considering how they respond to any artificially imposed intervention (that would be another review in itself).
Comparison: Could be between caregivers (e.g. those caregiving for people with different conditions) and non-carers. It is essential that all caregivers being considered had a mean age of 75.
Focus on caregiver experience which could cover a range of aspects:
caregivers perceived their role;
their caregiving duties;
caregivers health and wellbeing;
caregiving relationships;

Medline (1985 – May 2019), PsychINFO (1985– May 2019), Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL Plus, 1985 – May 2019), Embase (1985– May 2019), Sociological Abstracts (1985– May 2019), Social Service Abstracts (1985- May 2019)
Reference search of papers included after full-title search
Citation search (reference chaining) of papers included after full-title search.
Grey literature will not be searched as it is empirical academic research that is the focus of the paper.
Limits: Human, English-only, peer-reviewed, published empirical research, 1985-
Modified PRISMA to present search strategy
Types of studies included
We will include qualitative, quantiative and mixed-methods studies. All relevant reviews (literature, meta or systematic) will also be included. Case studies will be included

One review author (TM) wil screen the titles and remove duplicates. TM will then screen titles and abstracts for relevance and judge eligibility of the studies. AB will screen 10% of abstracts. TM and AB will use Rayyan application to aid independent screening of abstracts and full-text papers. TM will screen all full-text papers and AB will screen a third. All papers that are included will be re-read by TM to AB as a final check for their legitimate inclusion. At any point where outcome is unclear they will consult between each other and with RD and SB.
Risk of bias (quality) assessment

Gough’s weight of evidence (2007) a widely used tool suitable for qualitative and quantitative studies. This process involved rating studies ‘high’, ‘medium’ or ‘low’ in relation to the three categories A) generic quality of each studies, B) their specific appropriateness to the review, and C) their utility. The ‘quality’ of each study was awarded on the basis of the average of the individual scores (if two highs and a medium study was marked high) (see Table 2) and is represented under the category ‘D’.
A feminist quality appraisal tool (Morgan, 2016) along with critical interpretive synthesis (Dixon, 2006)

This narrative synthesis intertwined three main elements of Popay (2006) and colleagues’ approach: developing a preliminary synthesis, exploring relationships within the data and assessing the robustness of the synthesis.

We conducted a thematic analysis that focused on the “main, recurrent and/or most important (based on the review question) themes and/or concepts across multiple studies”. Through this process we identified three overarching themes. These are presented below. To further protect against bias, a modified version of the vote-counting process was used to determine whether each theme was supported, negated or irrelevant to each included study in turn. Relevant insights from this process, particularly the cases of conflicting findings, were subsequently incorporated into the synthesis. Themes were frequently discussed between TM, AB, SB and RD to aid transparency and reliably of their production.
